    Summary and Schedule

    Workshop Overview

    This workshop is about running machine learning and AI work on AWS without losing control of the bill: where the data goes, which machine does what, how a job is launched and paid for, and how to find out what it cost. It is in four parts.

    Part 1, orientation. What the cloud offers a researcher compared with a laptop or the cluster down the hall, and what it costs. The two services the lesson uses: SageMaker rents machines by the second, for a notebook you work in and for jobs that run on their own and end; Bedrock serves hosted models by the token, with nothing to start or stop. The four things every episode uses, S3, a notebook instance, jobs and Bedrock, and how every later episode estimates and checks what a job costs.

    Part 2, SageMaker: data, training, fine-tuning and tuning.

    • Put the data in an S3 bucket and start a small notebook instance that launches everything else. The notebook is the controller, not the workhorse: the expensive compute runs on instances SageMaker rents for each job and releases when it ends.
    • Train XGBoost and PyTorch models on the Titanic data as training jobs. Estimate the cost before each launch and read the billable seconds after, compare a CPU instance with a GPU, and see what two instances buy and what they do not.
    • Fine-tune a 3B open-weight vision-language model with LoRA, as a training job with checkpoints and a runtime cap, for transcribing handwritten German letters (Badger Scribe), scored on held-out pages before and after.
    • Run a hyperparameter tuning job that trains ten models under a budget set up front.

    Part 3, Bedrock: inference and retrieval-augmented generation.

    • Build a RAG pipeline over a corpus of energy research papers (WattBot): embed the papers, retrieve, generate, score. The models are Bedrock’s, paid per token through tagged inference profiles so the spend has an owner, and the whole run costs cents.
    • Add multimodal embeddings for the questions whose answers live in tables and figures, and measure what they change.
    • Run the same pipeline with an open-weight model Bedrock does not serve, as SageMaker Processing jobs that rent a GPU for the minutes they need; optionally, the same on a notebook GPU, as the comparison.

    Part 4, resource management and cleanup. What to stop, what to delete, how to read the bill, and the rules the account enforces on every launch, with how to set the same rules on an account of your own. An optional episode shows the same jobs from a terminal.

    Who this workshop is for

    Researchers and students who use ML or AI in their work and want or need to run it in the cloud. The lesson assumes a basic machine learning background: you know what training, hyperparameter tuning, fine-tuning, embeddings and retrieval-augmented generation are. It does not teach these concepts; instructors may briefly review some of them depending on the audience, but the default schedule does not include that time. Python and Jupyter are used throughout; no prior AWS experience is needed.

    Cost controls

    The cloud is often very affordable for research workloads, and this lesson shows it: run as written, the whole workshop, training jobs, a tuning job, a LoRA fine-tune on a GPU and two RAG pipelines, costs each learner a few dollars. Every episode tags its resources, caps job runtime, estimates cost before launching and checks the bill after, and cleans up. The final episode covers monitoring and cleanup, and the rules a shared account can enforce.

    What This Workshop Does Not Cover

    • General ML/AI concepts: the focus is on moving existing ML and AI work to the cloud, not on teaching training, fine-tuning or RAG themselves.
    • Deploying models as endpoints: serving a trained or fine-tuned model behind an always-on API.
    • Agents and tool use: LLM applications that call tools or chain multiple model calls (e.g., Bedrock Agents).

    If there’s a specific ML or AI workflow or AWS service you’d like to see included in this curriculum, please let us know! We’re happy to develop additional content to meet the needs of researchers, students, and ML/AI practitioners. Please post an issue on the lesson GitHub or contact endemann@wisc.edu with suggestions or requests.

    Duration: 00h 00m  1. Overview: ML on AWS When is cloud compute the right tool for a researcher who already has a cluster or a workstation?
    What do SageMaker and Bedrock add on top of renting a machine?
    Duration: 00h 15m  2. Data Storage: Setting up S3 How can I store and manage data effectively in AWS for SageMaker workflows?
    What are the best practices for using S3 versus EC2 storage for machine learning projects?
    Duration: 00h 35m  3. Notebooks as Controllers How do you set up and use SageMaker notebooks for machine learning tasks?
    How can you manage compute resources efficiently using SageMaker’s controller notebook approach?
    Duration: 00h 55m  4. Accessing and Managing Data in S3 with SageMaker Notebooks How can I load data from S3 into a SageMaker notebook?
    How do I monitor storage usage and costs for my S3 bucket?
    What steps are involved in pushing new data back to S3 from a notebook?
    Duration: 01h 25m  5. (Optional) Pushing Your Notebooks to GitHub from SageMaker How can I put the code I write on a SageMaker notebook instance under version control on GitHub?
    How do I authenticate to GitHub from a notebook instance without leaving a password or key behind?
    How can I convert notebooks to .py files and keep .ipynb files out of version control?
    Duration: 02h 00m  6. Training Models in SageMaker: Intro What are the differences between local training and SageMaker-managed training?
    What is a SageMaker training job, and what does it cost?
    How do you estimate what a training job will cost before launching it, and check what it cost afterwards?
    Duration: 03h 05m  7. Training Models in SageMaker: PyTorch Example When should you consider using a GPU instance for training neural networks in SageMaker, and what are the benefits and limitations?
    How does SageMaker handle data parallelism and model parallelism, and which is suitable for typical neural network training?
    Duration: 03h 55m  8. Fine-tuning a Vision-Language Model with Training Jobs When is fine-tuning worth it?
    What does a fine-tuning run cost, and how do I estimate that before launching it?
    How do I fine-tune a model as a SageMaker training job?
    How do I tell whether the fine-tune helped?
    Duration: 06h 55m  9. Hyperparameter Tuning in SageMaker: Neural Network Example How can we efficiently manage hyperparameter tuning in SageMaker?
    How can we parallelize tuning jobs to optimize time without increasing costs?
    Duration: 07h 55m 10. Overview of RAG Workflows on AWS What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
    What are the four ways to run inference on AWS, and which does a RAG pipeline need?
    Why is Bedrock the default, and when is SageMaker the right choice instead?
    How do the billing models differ, and what does it cost to forget to shut something down?
    Duration: 08h 10m 11. RAG with Bedrock How do we build a complete RAG pipeline on AWS without provisioning a GPU?
    How do we turn a collection of PDFs into retrievable, citable chunks stored in S3?
    How do we call Bedrock-hosted embedding and generation models so that the spend is tagged to our project?
    Duration: 09h 00m 12. RAG with Processing Jobs When does a RAG pipeline need a self-hosted, open-weight model instead of Bedrock?
    How do we run the embedding and generation steps of the WattBot pipeline as SageMaker Processing jobs that end on their own?
    How do we pass data in and out of a job through S3, and tag the job so its cost is traceable?
    Duration: 09h 50m 13. (Optional) RAG with a Notebook GPU How can we run a basic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline entirely from a single GPU-backed SageMaker notebook?
    How do we go from cached text chunks to a searchable embedding space using a self-hosted model?
    How can we generate WattBot-style answers (including citations and evidence) that follow the competition’s scoring conventions?
    Duration: 10h 35m 14. (Optional) The Same Jobs from the Terminal What does the AWS command-line interface (CLI) let me do that the lesson’s notebooks did, and what should I not do with it?
    How do I see, and stop, everything that is costing money from a terminal?
    What request does the SageMaker SDK send when I call estimator.fit()?
    Duration: 11h 05m 15. Resource Management and Monitoring How can I monitor and manage AWS resources to avoid unnecessary costs?
    What steps are necessary to clean up SageMaker and S3 resources after the workshop?
    What best practices can help with efficient resource utilization?

    Setup (Complete Before The Workshop)

    Before the workshop:

    1. GitHub Account (optional) – Only needed for the optional episode on pushing your own code to GitHub.
    2. AWS Access – Use a shared AWS account (UW-Madison) or an AWS account of your own.
    3. Data – Download one small zip.
    4. Glossary — Skim the workshop glossary.
    5. Episodes 1 to 4 first — They create the bucket and notebook instance every later episode uses.

    Details on each step are outlined below.

    1. GitHub Account (optional)

    Only needed for the optional episode on pushing your notebooks to GitHub. Sign up if you plan to do it.

    2. AWS Account

    There are two ways to get access to AWS for this lesson. Please wait for a pre-workshop email from the instructor to confirm which option to choose.

    If you are attending this lesson at UW-Madison, the instructors will provide a shared AWS account for all attendees. You do not need to set up your own AWS account. What to expect:

    • Stick to the lesson materials, so that expensive pipelines (e.g., training/tuning LLMs) do not lead to high costs and wasted credits.
    • Do not use any tools we do not explicitly cover without discussing with the instructors first.
    • Stop (and at the end of the workshop, delete) every notebook instance you create. A GPU notebook left running costs about $60 a day.
    • Before the workshop, the instructor adds you to the shared account and emails you a sign-in link. It opens the AWS console directly in the workshop account and role after you sign in with your UW–Madison NetID. Bookmark it; it is the link you will use every session. The link is sent by email rather than posted here on purpose: treat it like any other sign-in page and only use the one your instructor sent.
    • Verify your access before the workshop: open the link and sign in. If you see a “no access” or “not assigned” message, email the instructor with your username. Check that the account name and region in the top-right of the console match the email.
    • Three rules on the shared account:
      • Stick to the lesson materials, so that expensive pipelines (e.g., training/tuning LLMs) do not lead to high costs and wasted credits.
      • Do not use any tools we do not explicitly cover without discussing with the instructors first.
      • Stop (and at the end of the workshop, delete) every notebook instance you create. A GPU notebook left running costs about $60 a day.
    • The account enforces a short list of rules on every launch (the three cost tags with values from fixed lists, the lesson’s instance types, a 48-hour cap, no endpoints). A job that breaks one is refused with an AccessDenied message that does not say why; If a Launch Is Refused does, and the lesson’s helper module can tell you before and after the launch. Check there before emailing.

    If you are not attending through the shared account, follow these steps:

    1. Create an account at aws.amazon.com on the paid plan. Since July 2025 new accounts start on a free plan limited to a set of free-tier services, which does not cover GPU instances.
    2. Everything in the workshop is billed. Following the materials end to end costs about $10: the Titanic episodes a few dollars, the Bedrock episode cents, the Processing Jobs episode under a dollar, the fine-tuning episode about $0.75 in class plus about $1.50 for the optional homework. The one way to spend much more is to leave a GPU notebook instance running: about $60 a day. Set a Budgets alert at $50 before you start.
    3. Request GPU quotas three to four weeks before the workshop. New accounts have a quota of 0 for GPU instances, and increases can take weeks. In the console, go to Service Quotas → Amazon SageMaker and request: ml.g5.xlarge for training job usage (1), ml.g4dn.xlarge for training job usage (1), ml.g5.xlarge for processing job usage (2), and ml.g6e.xlarge for notebook instance usage (1, optional GPU-notebook episode only). A justification like “self-paced machine learning workshop” is enough.
    4. Check under Amazon Bedrock → Model access that the RAG episode’s models, DeepSeek V3 and Titan Text Embeddings V2, show as available in your region. Bedrock enables its serverless models automatically; only Anthropic’s need a use-case form.
    5. Stage the shared datasets yourself, since there is no instructor bucket: the WattBot files for the RAG episodes, and the Badger Scribe data and the CHURRO-3B weights for the fine-tuning episode. The commands are in the lesson’s instructor page Shared data bucket: staging before each term; set shared_bucket in those episodes to your own bucket.

    Once your AWS account is set up, log in to the AWS Management Console. For the shared account that means the sign-in link from your instructor’s email, of the form https://<org>.awsapps.com/start/#/console?account_id=...&role_name=...; for your own account, the regular console sign-in at https://console.aws.amazon.com/.

    3. Download the Data

    1. Download data.zip (Right-click -> Save as).
    2. Extract it (Right-click -> Extract all on Windows; double-click on Mac).
    3. Keep the two Titanic files somewhere you can find them during the S3 episode, e.g.
    • ~/Downloads/data/titanic/titanic_train.csv
    • ~/Downloads/data/titanic/titanic_test.csv

    4. Review the Workshop Glossary Page

    Skim the Glossary before the workshop (it is also in the top menu of every lesson page); the terms come up from the first episode.

    5. Episodes 1 to 4 come first

    The first four episodes are the setup for everything after them, and the instructor walks through them with the class rather than leaving them as reading. Episode 2 creates the S3 bucket that every later episode writes to, and episode 3 creates the notebook instance and clones this lesson’s repository onto it, which is where the prefilled notebooks for every episode come from: each later episode opens with “Open the notebook from /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/...”, and that folder exists only once episode 3 has been done. Episode 4 is where the notebook first reads your bucket, with the helper that every later data step uses.

    If you want to jump ahead to a later episode, do episodes 1 to 4 first on the instance you will use, and then start wherever you like. After that, the training episodes 6, 7 and 9 are a sequence (the tuning episode, 9, uses the files 7 saves), the fine-tuning episode 8 stands on its own, and the RAG episodes (10 to 13) are a sequence, since each one reuses what the one before it cached in your bucket.
